"Missing" is a song by British musical duo Everything but the Girl from their eighth studio album, Amplified Heart (1994). It was written by the two band members, Tracey Thorn and Ben Watt, and was produced by the duo with John Coxon. It was released as the album's second single on 8 August 1994, promoted as an extended play (EP). The song initially did not achieve much success until it was remixed by Todd Terry and re-released in 1995, resulting in worldwide success, peaking at or near the top of the charts in many countries. The release of the remixed version of "Missing" gave an indication of the band's future experimentation with more electronic dance music on subsequent albums. Its music video was directed by Mark Szaszy.

Musically the song takes in multiple genres. The original version from the album is a more low-tempo influenced song, while the popular Todd Terry remix version is a more up-tempo dance-pop song. "Missing" was critically acclaimed by the majority of music critics, who praised the composition and generally considered it a highlight on the album. In 2022 and 2025, Rolling Stone and Billboard magazine included it in their lists of the greatest dance songs of all time.[3][4]

Background

Prior to "Missing", Everything but the Girl was known as an indie band. Their music had folk and jazz leanings. They had released eight albums prior to Amplified Heart and had a number-three UK singles chart success in 1988 ("I Don't Want to Talk About It"), but were relatively unknown in the United States.

Amplified Heart, marked a more introspective and stripped-back approach compared with Everything but the Girl’s earlier work, featuring minimalist arrangements and emotionally restrained performances. "Missing" was recorded in London between December 1993 and April 1994 as a relaxed-sounding guitar-based popular music song that had earned modest broadcasting airplay on US Adult Contemporary radio. The duo gave the track to house music producer Todd Terry to remix for nightclubs.[5]

Tracey Thorn later explained to Rolling Stone that the song was originally intended as a dance-oriented track:[6]

It was written with that idea in mind, totally... we put on sort of a laid back house groove instead. Then when we gave it to Todd, he took it in a really, really strong New York house direction, which had a real simplicity to it, but it was very infectious.

According to the music sheet published at Musicnotes.com by Sony/ATV Music Publishing, "Missing" is written in the key of A minor.[7] In vocal range, Thorn's vocals span from the key note of E4 to the key note of G5.[7] The song is set in common time and has a beat of 128 beats per minute.[7] Lauren Barnett from The Guardian recalled the style of music as "monochrome electronic beats."[8] Toponehitwonders.com had said the remix "Add[s] a pulsing disco beat that sounds equally at home."

Critical reception

The song was generally acclaimed by most music critics. Larry Flick from Billboard magazine wrote, "This forlorn love song is bolstered by a springy retro-pop arrangement that is brilliantly tweaked into a credible dance confection by post-producer Todd Terry. Singer Tracey Thorn's performance is a study in affecting, but restrained emotion, and the chorus instantly sticks to the brain."[9] Steve Baltin from Cash Box noted that here, the duo "throw in everything but the sink", concluding with that "the blend is very effective, though, as the song comes off as a mix between Lisa Stansfield and Cowboy Junkies. Ethereal pop that can be danced to isn't much in demand these days, but this winner could change that if given the opportunity."[10] Douglas Wolk from CMJ said it's "a first-rate pairing of songwriting and technology", pairing a torch song and techno-inflected backing tracks. He added that "neither the song nor the grooves are all that hot on their own, but in combination they're great—the kind of heartfelt but not histrionic dancefloor simmer that's been too rare since, say, Lisa Stansfield's heyday a few years ago."[11]

Dave Sholin from the Gavin Report commented, "What a difference a few months and a remix can make. Miami is where 'Missing' has busted big, and where requests tell the story of how broad the appeal of the song really is. Track two, the remix edit, is the one to check out."[12] Chuck Campbell from Knoxville News Sentinel felt it "achieves a beautifully enchanting chorus".[13] Pan-European magazine Music & Media wrote, "Suddenly hip in the dance milieu due to Tracey Thorn's vocals on Massive Attacks 'Protection', these remixes by Todd Terry and Ultramarine a.o. will further speed it up."[14] James Hamilton from Music Week's RM Dance Update described it as "atmospheric" and "melancholy" in his weekly dance column.[15] Ben Turner from Muzik considered it a "miracle".[16] John Kilgo from The Network Forty named it a "very exciting uptempo groover from this debut artist."[17] James Hunter from Vibe remarked that Terry's remix had allowed singer Tracey Thorn "to grace stateside radios with her rare English soul", adding that her voice "is untouchable".[18]

Retrospective response

Bill Lamb from About.com said that "there has never been a more powerful expression of emotional and sexual longing in pop music than that at the core of 'Missing'."[19] AllMusic was also very positive, highlighting the song as an album standout and rated it with 4 stars out of 5.[20][21] Stopera and Galindo from BuzzFeed ranked it number 10 in their list of "The 101 Greatest Dance Songs of the '90s" in 2017, commenting, "Have you ever sat and really thought about if the desert actually misses the rain? Like any good song, it makes you think."[22] A writer from Complex noted that the remix "set the world ablaze".[23] Idolator ranked it among "The 50 Best Pop Singles of 1995", calling the song a "noir-ish study in wistful longing, with a hint of lonely-but-relatable stalker in the lyric."[24]

Chart performance

The resulting Todd Terry remixed dance version of "Missing" became a worldwide success, matching Everything But the Girl's best UK chart score of number three in November 1995[25] and scoring number one on the German singles chart. The song became the duo's first and only US Top 40 entry on the Billboard Hot 100, entering at number 94 for the week ending 12 August 1995.[26] After a long climb, it peaked at number two during 1996 (in its 28th chart week). "Missing" eventually logged 55 weeks on the chart (a record at the time which has since been broken; the single is today the eleventh-longest charting song on the US Hot 100). "Missing" was the first ever single to spend an uninterrupted year on the US Hot 100.[27] It also topped the US Cash Box Top 100. Even with its success in the mainstream and in nightclubs, the remix never entered the US Hot Dance Club Play chart.

In addition to its US success, "Missing" topped the Canadian RPM Top Singles, Adult Contemporary, and Dance/Urban charts. In the UK it spent over 20 weeks on the UK Singles Chart and earned the duo a double platinum certification from the British Phonographic Industry (BPI), denoting sales and streams of over 1,200,000 units. The song was also successful in Australia and New Zealand. It peaked at number two in Australia, staying on the chart for twenty-three weeks. It had similar success in New Zealand, peaking at 14 on the charts and stayed in the charts for fourteen weeks. The song also eventually peaked inside the top ten in many European countries, including Austria, Belgium (Flanders and Wallonia), France, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and Switzerland. In Latin America, it became a top-10 hit in El Salvador.[28] The single has sold three million copies worldwide.[29]

Music video

An accompanying music video was shot for the single (both the original and dance versions). It was directed by English director Mark Szaszy.[30] The video features both Thorn and Watt in an apartment, having split up but them missing each other. It also features Thorn walking around Balham and Clapham South.[31]

Impact and legacy

In 2003, Q Magazine ranked "Missing" at number 177 in their list of the "1001 Best Songs Ever".[32] Same year, English music journalist Paul Morley included it in his list of "Greatest Pop Single of All Time".[33] In 2011, Fedde le Grand remixed the song and DJ Ron Slomowicz from About.com listed the track as the "Song of the Day". He said "Tracey's mournful voice fit perfectly over Todd's house beats to become a club classic and a pop hit around the world."[34] Bill Lamb from the same publication ranked the song at top spot on his "Top 10 Best Songs of 1996".[35] He later reviewed the remix, saying "pumps up the tempo, adds some beats but thankfully stays true to the original."[34] Toponehitwonders.com was very positive stating "'Missing' ... is a tremendous pop song. One of the best of the 1990s. In fact, I would place it in the same company as 'You Get What You Give' by New Radicals as a nearly perfect pop song." They later complimented the chorus, catchy hook and vocal performance by Thorn.[36]

In 2012, the song was listed at number 35 in NME's list of the "50 Best-Selling Tracks of the 90s", adding: "The 1994 version of 'Missing' had at least a foot on the dancefloor - in defiance of EBTG style - but Todd Terry gave it the final push, his deep house beats complementing Tracey Thorn's rich melancholy pine. Slowly burning, it spent five months on the UK chart and an entire year on the Billboard Hot 100. Sold: 870,000"[37] In 2018, ThoughtCo ranked the song number one in their list of "10 Best Pop Songs of 1996".[38] In 2022, Pitchfork featured it on their lists of "The 30 Best House Tracks of the '90s" and "The 250 Best Songs of the 1990s",[39][2] while Classic Pop ranked it number nine in their list of the top 40 dance tracks from the '90s.[40] The same year, Rolling Stone ranked "Missing" number 54 in their "200 Greatest Dance Songs of All Time".[3] In 2025, Billboard magazine ranked it number 25 in their list of "The 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time", writing, "If Everything But the Girl were standing by the edge of the pool, mulling a swim, Todd Terry came along and shoved them in."[4]

In 1995, Germany-based music trio No Mercy released their version of "Missing" with the subtitle "I Miss You Like the Deserts Miss the Rain". It was produced by Frank Farian and appeared on their debut album, My Promise (1996), and its North American counterpart, No Mercy. Stylistically, the cover is largely based on the remix by Todd Terry. It was a moderate hit, peaking within the top 20 in Germany and top 10 in Switzerland. In the music video, the band members of No Mercy are looking for a woman.[146]

Girl song)|Walking Wounded]] | next_year = 1996 | misc = {{External music video|{{YouTube|IAkY5m00rpY|"Missing" (Todd Terry remix)}}}} }} "'''Missing'''" is a song by British musical duo [[Everything but the Girl]] from their eighth studio album, ''[[Amplified Heart]]'' (1994). It was written by the two band members, [[Tracey Thorn]] and [[Ben Watt]], and was produced by the duo with John Coxon. It was released as the album's second single on 8 August 1994, promoted as an [[extended play]] (EP). The song initially did not achieve much success until it was remixed by [[Todd Terry]] and re-released in 1995, resulting in worldwide success, peaking at or near the top of the charts in many countries. The release of the remixed version of "Missing" gave an indication of the band's future experimentation with more [[electronic dance music]] on subsequent albums. Its music video was directed by Mark Szaszy. Musically the song takes in multiple genres. The original version from the album is a more low-tempo influenced song, while the popular Todd Terry remix version is a more up-tempo [[dance-pop]] song. "Missing" was critically acclaimed by the majority of music critics, who praised the composition and generally considered it a highlight on the album. In 2022 and 2025, ''[[Rolling Stone magazine|Rolling Stone]]'' and ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine included it in their lists of the greatest dance songs of all time.{{cite magazine|first1=Jon|last1=Dolan|first2=Julyssa|last2=Lopez|first3=Michaelangelo|last3=Matos|first4=Claire|last4=Shaffer|title=200 Greatest Dance Songs of All Time|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/200-greatest-dance-songs-of-all-time-1372888/green-velvet-flash-1995-1376976/|magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]|date=22 July 2022|accessdate=30 October 2022}}{{cite magazine|first1=Andrea|last1=Domanick|first2=Andrew|last2=Unterberger|first3=Elias|last3=Leight|first4=Eric|last4=Renner Brown|first5=Jason|last5=Lipshutz|first6=Joe|last6=Lynch|first7=Kat|last7=Bein|first8=Katie|last8=Bein|first9=Krystal|last9=Rodriguez|first10=Lily|last10=Moayeri|first11=Melinda|last11=Newman|first12=Thomas|last12=Smith|first13=Zei|last13=McCarthy|url=https://www.billboard.com/lists/best-dance-songs-all-time/|title=The 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time: Staff List|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=28 March 2025|access-date=6 April 2025}} ==Background== Prior to "Missing", Everything but the Girl was known as an indie band. Their music had [[folk music|folk]] and [[jazz music|jazz]] leanings. They had released eight albums prior to ''Amplified Heart'' and had a number-three [[UK singles chart]] success in 1988 ("[[I Don't Want to Talk About It#Everything but the Girl version|I Don't Want to Talk About It]]"), but were relatively unknown in the United States. ''Amplified Heart'', marked a more introspective and stripped-back approach compared with Everything but the Girl’s earlier work, featuring minimalist arrangements and emotionally restrained performances. "Missing" was recorded in London between December 1993 and April 1994 as a relaxed-sounding guitar-based popular music song that had earned modest broadcasting airplay on US Adult Contemporary radio. The duo gave the track to [[house music]] producer [[Todd Terry]] to [[remix]] for nightclubs.{{cite web |last=Ryan |first=Chris |title=Everything But the Girl: Amplified Heart|website=Pitchfork |date=30 April 2014 |url=https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/everything-but-the-girl-amplified-heart/ |access-date=23 December 2025}} [[Tracey Thorn]] later explained to ''[[Rolling Stone magazine|Rolling Stone]]'' that the song was originally intended as a dance-oriented track:{{cite news|first=Christopher G|last=Feldman|title=The Billboard Book of No. 2 Singles|isbn=0-8230-7695-4|publisher=Billboard books|year=2000|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/billboardbookofn00chri}} {{quote|It was written with that idea in mind, totally... we put on sort of a laid back house groove instead. Then when we gave it to Todd, he took it in a really, really strong New York house direction, which had a real simplicity to it, but it was very infectious.}} ==Composition== {{Listen | type = music | filename = Everything But The Girl - Missing (Todd Terry Club Mix).ogg | title = Everything but the Girl – "Missing" (Todd Terry club mix) }} According to the music sheet published at Musicnotes.com by [[Sony/ATV Music Publishing]], "Missing" is written in the key of [[A minor]].{{cite web|url=http://www.musicnotes.com/sheetmusic/mtdFPE.asp?ppn=MN0056078|title=Missing by Everything But The Girl - Digital Sheet Music|publisher=Musicnotes.com|access-date=10 February 2014}} In vocal range, Thorn's vocals span from the key note of E4 to the key note of G5. The song is set in [[common time]] and has a beat of 128 beats per minute. Lauren Barnett from ''[[The Guardian]]'' recalled the style of music as "monochrome electronic beats."{{cite news|author=Laura Barnett|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2012/jun/17/everything-but-girl-early-albums-interview|title=Everything But the Girl: 'You feel like you're listening to a different person'|newspaper=The Guardian|access-date=10 February 2014}} ''Toponehitwonders.com'' had said the remix "Add[s] a pulsing disco beat that sounds equally at home." ==Critical reception== The song was generally acclaimed by most music critics. [[Larry Flick]] from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine wrote, "This forlorn love song is bolstered by a springy retro-pop arrangement that is brilliantly tweaked into a credible dance confection by post-producer [[Todd Terry]]. Singer [[Tracey Thorn]]'s performance is a study in affecting, but restrained emotion, and the chorus instantly sticks to the brain."{{cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Billboard/90s/1994/BB-1994-12-10.pdf|first=Larry|last=Flick|title=Billboard: Single Reviews|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=10 December 1994|access-date=23 January 2018|author-link=Larry Flick}} Steve Baltin from ''[[Cash Box (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' noted that here, the duo "throw in everything but the sink", concluding with that "the blend is very effective, though, as the song comes off as a mix between [[Lisa Stansfield]] and [[Cowboy Junkies]]. Ethereal pop that can be danced to isn't much in demand these days, but this winner could change that if given the opportunity."{{cite magazine|first=Steve|last=Baltin|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/90s/1994/CB-1994-12-03.pdf|title=Pop Singles — Reviews|magazine=[[Cash Box (magazine)|Cash Box]]|date=3 December 1994|page=|accessdate=11 March 2022}} Douglas Wolk from ''[[CMJ]]'' said it's "a first-rate pairing of songwriting and technology", pairing a [[torch song]] and [[techno]]-inflected backing tracks. He added that "neither the song nor the grooves are all that hot on their own, but in combination they're great—the kind of heartfelt but not histrionic dancefloor simmer that's been too rare since, say, Lisa Stansfield's heyday a few years ago."{{cite magazine|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JC0EAAAAMBAJ|title=Singles|magazine=[[CMJ]]|date=1 January 1995|page=47|access-date=21 March 2020}} Dave Sholin from the ''[[Gavin Report]]'' commented, "What a difference a few months and a remix can make. The song became the duo's first and only US Top 40 entry on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], entering at number 94 for the week ending 12 August 1995.{{cite magazine | url=http://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100/1995-08-12 | title=Billboard Hot 100 | magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] }} After a long climb, it peaked at number two during 1996 (in its 28th chart week). "Missing" eventually logged 55 weeks on the chart (a record at the time which has since been broken; the single is today the eleventh-longest charting song on the US Hot 100). "Missing" was the first ever single to spend an uninterrupted year on the US Hot 100.{{Cite web|url=https://www.songfacts.com/facts/everything-but-the-girl/missing|title=Missing by Everything but the Girl - Songfacts|website=www.songfacts.com}} It also topped the US [[Cash Box Top 100 Pop Singles|''Cash Box'' Top 100]]. Even with its success in the mainstream and in nightclubs, the remix never entered the US [[Hot Dance Club Songs|Hot Dance Club Play]] chart. In addition to its US success, "Missing" topped the Canadian ''[[RPM (magazine)|RPM]]'' Top Singles, Adult Contemporary, and Dance/Urban charts. In the UK it spent over 20 weeks on the [[UK Singles Chart]] and earned the duo a double platinum certification from the [[British Phonographic Industry]] (BPI), denoting sales and streams of over 1,200,000 units. The song was also successful in Australia and New Zealand. It peaked at number two in Australia, staying on the chart for twenty-three weeks. It had similar success in New Zealand, peaking at 14 on the charts and stayed in the charts for fourteen weeks. The song also eventually peaked inside the top ten in many European countries, including Austria, Belgium ([[Flanders]] and [[Wallonia]]), France, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and Switzerland. In Latin America, it became a top-10 hit in El Salvador.{{cite journal|url=http://h.elsiglodetorreon.com.mx/Default/Scripting/ArticleWin.asp?From=Search&Key=EDT/1995/10/13/36/Ar03602.xml&CollName=EDT_1990_1999&DOCID=1935088&PageLabelPrint=36&skin=ElSiglo&sLanguage=English&Content=ALL&selLanguage=&sPublication=EDT&sDateFrom=01%252F01%252F1995&sDateTo=12%252F31%252F1995&dummy=1995&sQuery=yuri&x=11&y=1&RefineQueryView=&StartFrom=85&ViewMode=HTML|title=Discos más populares en Latinoamérica|journal=[[El Siglo de Torreón]]|date=13 October 1995|page=36|access-date=19 October 2026|language=es}} The single has sold three million copies worldwide.{{Cite web|url=http://thequietus.com/articles/09091-everything-but-the-girl-interview|title = The Quietus | Features | A Quietus Interview | from Eden with Love: Everything but the Girl Interviewed| date=19 June 2012 }} ==Music video== An accompanying music video was shot for the single (both the original and dance versions). It was directed by English director Mark Szaszy.{{cite web|url=https://imvdb.com/video/everything-but-the-girl/missing-todd-terry-remix|title=Missing (Todd Terry Remix) (1994) by Everything But The Girl|publisher=IMVDb.com|access-date=18 October 2018}} The video features both Thorn and Watt in an apartment, having split up but them missing each other. It also features Thorn walking around [[Balham]] and [[Clapham South]].{{cite web|author=ON|url=http://www.dailymotion.com/video/x36618_everything-but-the-girl-missing_music|title=Everything but the girl - Missing - Video Dailymotion|publisher=Dailymotion.com|date=9 October 2007|access-date=10 February 2014}} ==Impact and legacy== In 2003, ''[[Q (magazine)|Q Magazine]]'' ranked "Missing" at number 177 in their list of the "1001 Best Songs Ever".{{Cite web|url=https://www.muzieklijstjes.nl/Q1001bestsongsever.htm|title=Q - 1001 best songs ever (2003)|website=www.muzieklijstjes.nl}} Same year, English music journalist [[Paul Morley]] included it in his list of "Greatest Pop Single of All Time".{{cite web|title=Paul Morley|access-date=27 February 2026|via=Rocklist|url=http://www.rocklistmusic.co.uk/steveparker/paulmorley.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060619105322/http://www.rocklistmusic.co.uk/steveparker/paulmorley.htm|url-status=usurped|archive-date=19 June 2006}} In 2011, [[Fedde le Grand]] remixed the song and DJ Ron Slomowicz from [[About.com]] listed the track as the "Song of the Day". He said "Tracey's mournful voice fit perfectly over Todd's house beats to become a club classic and a pop hit around the world."{{Cite web |url=http://dancemusic.about.com/b/2011/01/03/song-of-the-day-everything-but-the-girl-missing-fedde-le-grand-remix.htm |title=About.com. |access-date=26 October 2012 |archive-date=15 May 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515082730/http://dancemusic.about.com/b/2011/01/03/song-of-the-day-everything-but-the-girl-missing-fedde-le-grand-remix.htm |url-status=dead }} Bill Lamb from the same publication ranked the song at top spot on his "Top 10 Best Songs of 1996".[http://top40.about.com/od/top10lists/tp/1996top10.htm Top 10 Best Songs of 1996] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121110062340/http://top40.about.com/od/top10lists/tp/1996top10.htm |date=10 November 2012 }}. He later reviewed the remix, saying "pumps up the tempo, adds some beats but thankfully stays true to the original." In fact, I would place it in the same company as '[[You Get What You Give (song)|You Get What You Give]]' by [[New Radicals]] as a nearly perfect pop song." They later complimented the chorus, catchy hook and vocal performance by Thorn.{{cite web|url=http://toponehitwonders.com/pop/everything-but-the-girl-%E2%80%93-missing/|title=Everything But the Girl – Missing ||publisher=Toponehitwonders.com|access-date=10 February 2014}} In 2012, the song was listed at number 35 in ''[[NME]]'''s list of the "50 Best-Selling Tracks of the 90s", adding: "The 1994 version of 'Missing' had at least a foot on the dancefloor - in defiance of EBTG style - but Todd Terry gave it the final push, his [[deep house]] beats complementing Tracey Thorn's rich melancholy pine.
